prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
The transition of Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition (DFER) from controlled laboratory settings to "in-the-wild" environments has introduced a significant challenge: dataset noise. Current approaches typically treat "noise" as a monolithic entity, applying a single strategy to mitigate it. We identify this as a critical flaw. In reality, DFER datasets suffer from two distinct types of noise:
1.  **Objective Low-Quality Data:** Samples rendered unusable due to physical factors such as occlusion, extreme blur, or dim lighting.
2.  **Subjective Annotation Error:** Usable data that is mislabeled due to human factors, such as confirmation bias (over-interpreting expressions) or missing low-intensity emotions (labeling subtle emotions as "Neutral").
Existing methods fail to differentiate between these categories, leading to suboptimal training where unusable data is retained or usable data is discarded.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that significantly higher performance can be achieved by decoupling noise mitigation into two distinct, sequential processes tailored to the specific nature of the noise.

We hypothesize that:
1.  **Low-quality samples** should be identified via learnable importance weights and **pruned** entirely, as they offer no distinct feature signal.
2.  **Mislabeled samples** (which are otherwise high quality) should be identified via prediction consistency and **corrected** (relabeled), allowing the model to learn from their valid visual features.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We aim to develop a **Dynamic Dual-Stage Purification (D2SP)** framework. This will be a plug-and-play module designed to wrap around existing DFER backbones. The purification process will be dynamic, re-evaluating the dataset at every training epoch to refine the data as the model improves.

The workflow consists of two sequential stages:

### 1. Coarse-Grained Pruning (CGP)
The first stage targets the removal of objectively bad data (e.g., occlusions).
*   **Weight Computation Module:** We will insert a parallel branch into the network that computes a scalar "importance weight" for each sample based on its embedding.
*   **Weighted Loss & Pruning:** We will employ a weighted loss function. The intuition is that the model will naturally assign lower weights to samples that are hard to learn due to poor quality (high uncertainty).
*   **Action:** Samples falling below a learned confidence threshold will be dynamically pruned from the current epoch's training set.

### 2. Fine-Grained Correction (FGC)
The second stage targets the correction of annotation bias in the remaining "clean" data.
*   **Stability Monitoring:** We will track the model's predictions over a sliding window of past epochs. We postulate that if a model consistently predicts a specific class with high confidence, contradicting the ground truth label, the sample is likely mislabeled rather than low-quality.
*   **Dual-Dimension Check:** We will assess stability across two dimensions: the consistency of the predicted label and the stability of the probability scores.
*   **Action:** When a sample exhibits high stability in contradicting the ground truth, we will overwrite the original label with the model's predicted label (pseudo-labeling) for the training process.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Framework:** A novel taxonomy for DFER noise, distinguishing between objective data degradation and subjective annotation bias.
*   **Technical Novelty:** A dynamic, closed-loop training strategy that simultaneously reduces dataset size (via pruning) and improves dataset quality (via relabeling) without requiring external clean reference sets.
*   **Practical Utility:** A generalized, model-agnostic framework capable of enhancing the robustness of various existing DFER architectures against real-world data imperfections.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the Dynamic Dual-Stage Purification (D2SP) framework. The experiments were designed to test the framework's ability to mitigate two identified types of noise (low-quality data and annotation errors) in Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition (DFER) tasks.

* **Datasets:**
    *   **FERV39k:** A large-scale multi-scene dataset containing 38,935 video clips segmented into 22 distinct scenes. It is noted for high complexity and noise levels.
    *   **DFEW:** A large-scale database containing 16,372 video clips extracted from over 1,500 movies.
    *   **MAFW:** A large-scale multi-modal compound affective database containing 10,045 video-audio clips captured in the wild.

* **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **WAR:** Weighted Average Recall.
    *   **UAR:** Unweighted Average Recall.

* **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **ResNet18_LSTM:** ResNet18 backbone with LSTM temporal modeling.
    *   **ResNet50_LSTM:** ResNet50 backbone with LSTM temporal modeling.
    *   **VGG13_LSTM:** VGG13 backbone with LSTM temporal modeling.
    *   **VGG16_LSTM:** VGG16 backbone with LSTM temporal modeling.
    *   **Former-DFER:** A transformer-based DFER method utilizing spatial and temporal transformers.
    *   **ViT_LSTM:** Vision Transformer backbone with LSTM temporal modeling.

* **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Framework:** PyTorch.
    *   **Hardware:** NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPUs.
    *   **Input Configuration:** 16 frames per video clip.
    *   **Training Duration:** 200 epochs.
    *   **Optimizer:** Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with a momentum of 0.9.
    *   **Architecture Modification:** For all baseline models, an extra branch was added after the embedding layer for weight assessment (Coarse-Grained Pruning stage) without altering other components.
    *   **Loss Function:** Weighted Cross-Entropy (WCE) Loss.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Noise Characterization:**
*   We identified two specific types of noise in DFER datasets.
    *   **Type 1 (Low Quality):** Caused by occlusion, dim lighting, and blurriness. These renders samples unusable.
    *   **Type 2 (Wrong Annotation):** Caused by annotator confirmation bias (mislabeling exaggerated expressions based on previous samples) and low-intensity emotions (incorrectly labeled as 'Neutral').

**Performance Analysis Observations:**
*   The D2SP framework provided the most significant performance improvements on the FERV39k dataset (average WAR increase of 3.97%). This dataset was observed to have higher complexity and scene diversity compared to DFEW and MAFW.
*   On the DFEW dataset, the average improvement was more modest (1.67% WAR), which we attribute to the dataset having fewer annotation errors and a lower baseline error rate compared to FERV39k.
*   We observed that solely using Coarse-Grained Pruning (CGP) or Fine-Grained Correction (FGC) in isolation yielded lower performance gains than combining them.
*   We found that "Static Purification" (using only the purified dataset from a specific round for subsequent training without dynamic updates) resulted in a performance decline compared to the baseline. This indicates that initial purification is not consistently accurate and dynamic updating is required.

**Visual Analysis Observations:**
*   **Weight Distribution:** We visualized the weights assigned during the CGP stage. Samples characterized as low quality (e.g., severe blur or occlusion) were assigned consistently lower weights compared to high-quality samples.
*   **Correction Verification:** We visualized samples corrected during the FGC stage. We observed successful correction of labels from non-Neutral to corrected labels (e.g., Angry to Happy) and from Neutral to corrected labels (e.g., Neutral to Happy/Sad), addressing the "low intensity" noise issue.

**Hyperparameter Sensitivity:**
*   **Threshold $\lambda$ (CGP):** Excessively high values led to the removal of too much data, harming model fitting. Overly low values failed to prune enough low-quality data. Optimal values differed by dataset (0.7 for FERV39k, 0.6 for DFEW).
*   **Threshold $\tau$ (FGC):** High values reduced the number of corrections (missing mislabeled samples), while very low values caused overcorrection (introducing noise). Optimal values differed by dataset (0.2 for FERV39k, 0.4 for DFEW).
*   **Stability Epochs ($t$):** A shorter duration was found effective (3 epochs for FERV39k, 2 for DFEW). Prolonged stability assessments appeared to restrict learning potential and lead to overfitting on specific features.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current methodologies in Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition (DFER) have shifted from controlled laboratory environments to "in-the-wild" settings, introducing significant data complexity. While recent advancements focus on spatial-temporal feature extraction (using architectures like 3D CNNs and Transformers), they often overlook the heterogeneity of noise inherent in these datasets.

Crucially, existing research treats "noise" as a monolithic category. We argue that this is a fundamental flaw. Our preliminary analysis suggests that noise in DFER datasets is comprised of two distinct categories requiring opposing treatment strategies:
1.  **Low-Quality Data:** Objective degradation caused by occlusion, dim lighting, or blurriness. These samples contain no usable emotional information and should be discarded.
2.  **Wrong Annotations:** Subjective errors caused by annotator confirmation bias or the mislabeling of low-intensity emotions as "Neutral." These samples contain valid visual information but incorrect supervisory signals and should be corrected rather than discarded.

Failing to distinguish between these types leads to suboptimal training: models either learn from unusable data or discard valuable data that simply needs relabeling. We aim to solve this by explicitly decoupling noise mitigation into pruning and correction phases.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose the development of a **Dynamic Dual-Stage Purification (D2SP)** Framework. This system will function as a general, plug-and-play module that integrates with existing DFER backbones.

Our core hypothesis is that by implementing a two-stage filtering process within the training loop, we can dynamically purify the dataset in real-time.
1.  **Stage 1 (Coarse-Grained Pruning):** Will identify and remove samples with low objective quality (low weights).
2.  **Stage 2 (Fine-Grained Correction):** Will identify samples where the model's prediction is stable but disagrees with the ground truth, correcting the label rather than discarding the sample.

We hypothesize that this dynamic purification will allow the model to self-curate its training data, resulting in a dataset that is both high-quality (visually) and correctly labeled.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will implement the D2SP framework comprising two sequential stages: Coarse-Grained Pruning (CGP) and Fine-Grained Correction (FGC). This process will be dynamic, re-evaluating the dataset $D$ at each training epoch.

### 1. Coarse-Grained Pruning (CGP) Stage
The objective of this stage is to compute a learnable weight for each sample and prune those that fall below a confidence threshold, effectively removing low-quality data.

**Weight Computation Module:**
Let the dataset be denoted as $D_1 = [v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n]$. For a sample input $v_i$, we extract an embedding $x_i$. We will construct a specific branch consisting of a two-layer Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) to compute a scalar weight $w_i$ for the sample. The formulation will be:

$$
\boldsymbol{w}_i = \sigma \left( \boldsymbol{W}_2^T \mathrm{ReLU} \left( \boldsymbol{W}_1^T \boldsymbol{x}_i + b_1 \right) + b_2 \right)
$$

Where:
*   $\boldsymbol{x}_i$ is the input embedding vector.
*   $\boldsymbol{W}_1, b_1$ and $\boldsymbol{W}_2, b_2$ are the weights and biases of the first and second linear layers, respectively.
*   $\sigma$ is the Sigmoid activation function.

**Weighted Prediction and Pruning:**
Simultaneously, the embedding $\boldsymbol{x}_i$ passes to the classification layer $f(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \theta)$ to obtain the raw predicted probability $p_i$. We define the **weighted predicted score** $s_i^t$ at epoch $t$ as:

$$
s_i^t = w_i \times p_i
$$

To ensure stability, we will calculate the mean score $S_T$ across the preceding $t$ epochs:

$$
S_T = \frac{1}{t} \sum_{j=T-t+1}^{T} s_i^j
$$

We will then define a binary pruning decision variable $\alpha$ based on a confidence threshold $\lambda$:

$$
\alpha = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & \mathrm{if~} S_T > \lambda \\ 0, & \mathrm{otherwise} \end{array} \right.
$$

Samples where $\alpha=0$ constitute the pruned set $D_2$ (low quality), while samples where $\alpha=1$ form the coarse-grained clean dataset $D_3$, which proceeds to the next stage.

**Weighted Cross-Entropy Loss:**
To enforce the learning of these weights, we will replace the standard loss with a Weighted Cross-Entropy (WCE) Loss:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WCE}} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(w_i f(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \boldsymbol{\theta}), y)
$$

This formulation ensures that gradients are scaled by $w_i$. High-quality samples (lower loss, higher $w_i$) will contribute more to parameter updates, while low-quality samples will have their influence minimized.

### 2. Fine-Grained Correction (FGC) Stage
The FGC stage operates on dataset $D_3$. Here, we address the second type of noise (annotation bias) by correcting labels rather than discarding data. We posit that if a model consistently predicts a label different from the ground truth with high confidence, the ground truth is likely incorrect.

We will evaluate prediction stability across two dimensions over the past $t$ epochs.

**Dimension 1: Predicted Label Stability**
We check if the predicted label $y_i'$ has remained consistent:

$$
\forall t_1, t_2 \in \{T-t+1, \ldots, T\}, \quad y_i^{\prime(t_1)} = y_i^{\prime(t_2)}
$$

**Dimension 2: Prediction Score Stability**
We define $\Delta p$ as the difference between the average predicted probability for the model's predicted label ($\bar{p'}$) and the average predicted probability for the original ground truth label ($\bar{p}_{\mathrm{gt}}$):

$$
\bar{p'} = \frac{1}{t} \sum_{j=T-t+1}^{T} \mathbf{\mathit{p}}_i^{\prime(j)}, \quad \bar{p}_{\mathrm{gt}} = \frac{1}{t} \sum_{j=T-t+1}^{T} \mathbf{\mathit{p}}_{\mathrm{gt}}^{(j)}
$$
$$
\Delta \boldsymbol{p} = \bar{p'} - \bar{p}_{\mathrm{gt}}
$$

**Label Correction Mechanism:**
We define a correction threshold $\tau$. If the stability differential exceeds this threshold, we treat the model's prediction as the new ground truth. The decision variable $\beta$ is defined as:

$$
\beta = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & \mathrm{if~} \Delta p > \tau \\ 0, & \mathrm{otherwise} \end{array} \right.
$$

If $\beta=1$, we update the label $y_i$ to $y_i'$. If $\beta=0$, we retain the original label. This results in the final fine-grained clean dataset $D_4$, which is used for the training update in the current epoch.

## Expected Contribution
This research expects to deliver three primary contributions to the field of Affective Computing:

1.  **Theoretical Refinement of Noise:** We will formally categorize DFER noise into "low-quality" (requiring pruning) and "wrong annotation" (requiring correction), moving beyond the monolithic noise assumption in current literature.
2.  **Novel Framework Architecture:** The D2SP framework will provide a robust mechanism for simultaneous sample re-weighting and label correction. Unlike static filtering, our dynamic approach allows the purification process to improve as the model's representation capability matures during training.
3.  **Generalizability:** By designing D2SP as an auxiliary module involving a simple MLP branch and logic gates, we ensure it can be plugged into any existing DFER backbone (CNN, RNN, or Transformer-based) without requiring structural overhaul of the core feature extractors.

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.model: claude-sonnet-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
